title: 2nd Grade Place Value and Number Charts Worksheets (+ Free Quiz)
meta_title: 2nd Grade Place Value & Number Charts + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach 2nd grade place value with a hundreds chart: tens and ones, 3-digit numbers, expanded form and comparing, plus a free quiz and worksheets.
excerpt: A hundreds chart looks like a boring grid of numbers until a Grade 2 child spots the patterns hiding in it. Here is how I use number charts to make place value click, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write the number 234 on a scrap of paper and ask a Grade 2 child what the 2 means. A surprising number will say ‘two’ — not ‘two hundred’. That single gap is what all of Grade 2 place value is really about: teaching a child that where a digit sits decides how much it is worth. And the fastest tool I know for making that idea visible is not a textbook page — it is a plain number chart.

This is a practical guide to teaching 2nd grade place value using number charts and hundreds charts, covering tens and ones, 3-digit numbers, expanded form and comparing numbers. You need a printed hundreds chart, a handful of counters, and about ten minutes a day.

Start with tens and ones, not with 3-digit numbers

By Grade 2 most children can count to 100, but counting is not the same as understanding. The goal is for a child to see 34 as ‘3 tens and 4 ones’, not as thirty-four separate things. Bundle ten sticks with a rubber band, or use a ten-frame, and the abstract idea becomes something they can hold.

A quick check I use: ask a child to make 47 with ten-bundles and loose ones. If they reach for 47 loose counters instead of 4 bundles and 7 singles, they are still counting all — and that is exactly where the number chart earns its place.

Why a hundreds chart makes place value visible

A hundreds chart is a 10×10 grid running 1 to 100. Its magic is that place value is baked into its shape, and children discover this themselves if you let them.

  • Move one square right and the number goes up by 1 — the ones digit changes.
  • Move one square down and the number jumps by 10 — the tens digit changes, the ones stay put.
  • A whole column (like 4, 14, 24, 34…) shares the same ones digit.
  • A whole row shares the same tens digit.

Once a child notices that ‘down means plus ten’, mental addition of 10 stops needing any counting at all. That is a genuine shortcut they keep for years, and they feel clever for spotting it — which matters more than we admit at this age.

A chart game that actually teaches

Cover a number on the chart with a coin and ask the child what is hidden. To work it out they have to reason from the neighbours: the square above is ten less, the square to the left is one less. This is far better practice than reciting numbers, because it forces them to use the tens-and-ones structure instead of just reading it.

Growing into 3-digit numbers

Grade 2 in the NCERT sequence pushes past 100 to 3-digit numbers. The chart idea scales up cleanly: hundreds, tens and ones. The number 236 is 2 hundreds, 3 tens and 6 ones — and the safest way to show this is with place value blocks (flats for hundreds, rods for tens, cubes for ones) or a simple three-column place value chart.

Watch for the classic trap. A child who can read 236 may still write ‘two hundred and thirty-six’ as 20036 — literally 200, then 30, then 6 stuck together. That is not a silly error; it is a child taking ‘two hundred’ and ‘thirty’ and ‘six’ at face value. The fix is expanded form, done out loud, many times.

Expanded form: the sentence version of a number

Expanded form breaks a number into the value of each digit and adds them back:

NumberHundredsTensOnesExpanded form
47—40740 + 7
236200306200 + 30 + 6
30530005300 + 0 + 5
560500600500 + 60 + 0

Notice the two rows with a zero. Numbers like 305 and 560 are where place value is truly tested, because the zero is a placeholder doing real work — it holds the tens spot (or ones spot) open so the other digits stay in their lanes. Spend extra time on numbers with a zero in the middle or end; they catch out more Grade 2 children than any other kind.

Comparing numbers: read left to right

To compare two numbers, a child should compare the highest place value first. Is 253 bigger than 235? Both have 2 hundreds, so move on. 5 tens beats 3 tens, so 253 wins — the ones never even matter. Teaching ‘start from the left, stop at the first difference’ is far more reliable than the ‘bigger number has more digits’ rule of thumb, which quietly fails the moment two numbers have the same number of digits.

The crocodile mouth for < and > is fine as a memory hook, but insist the child says why first: ‘253 is greater because 5 tens beat 3 tens.’ The reasoning is the learning; the symbol is just shorthand.

A ten-minute weekly rhythm

Consistency beats marathon sessions at this age. A pattern that works for the Tier-2 city parents I have advised: two days on the hidden-number chart game, one day building 3-digit numbers with blocks, one day on expanded form, and the weekend on a mixed worksheet where the child has to switch between all of it. That switching is where you find out whether place value has actually stuck.

One honest caveat: do not rush a child onto 3-digit numbers because the textbook has moved on. If tens and ones are shaky, hundreds will collapse on top of them. A secure 47 is worth more than a wobbly 470.

Try the quiz, then the worksheets

The short quiz below covers exactly what we walked through — tens and ones, reading a hundreds chart, 3-digit numbers, expanded form and comparing. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable place value worksheets at the end give graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: 2nd Grade Place Value Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on tens and ones, hundreds charts, 3-digit numbers, expanded form and comparing. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 2 place value and number charts to 3 digits

questions.q: In the number 34, what does the 3 stand for?
questions.explanation: The 3 sits in the tens place, so it means 3 tens, which is 30. The 4 is 4 ones.

questions.q: On a hundreds chart, what happens when you move one square straight down?
questions.explanation: Moving down one row jumps by 10 — the tens digit changes and the ones digit stays the same.

questions.q: How many tens and ones are in 68?
questions.explanation: 68 is 6 tens (60) and 8 ones. Reading left to right, the first digit is tens.

questions.q: What is the expanded form of 236?
questions.explanation: The 2 is 2 hundreds (200), the 3 is 3 tens (30) and the 6 is 6 ones. So 236 = 200 + 30 + 6.
3 hundreds, 0 tens and 5 ones make 305. The zero holds the tens place open.
Both have 2 hundreds, so compare tens. 5 tens beats 3 tens, so 253 is greater.

questions.q: On a hundreds chart, the numbers 4, 14, 24 and 34 are all in the same column. What do they share?
questions.explanation: A column shares the same ones digit — here it is 4. A row shares the same tens digit.

questions.q: What is the value of the 5 in 560?
questions.explanation: The 5 is in the hundreds place, so it means 5 hundreds, which is 500.

faq.q: What place value should a 2nd grader know?
faq.a: By the end of Grade 2 a child should read and write numbers up to 3 digits, name the value of each digit (hundreds, tens, ones), write numbers in expanded form, and compare two numbers using the highest place value first.

faq.q: How does a hundreds chart help with place value?
faq.a: The chart makes the tens-and-ones structure visible: moving one square right adds 1 (ones), moving one square down adds 10 (tens). Children discover these patterns themselves, which makes adding and subtracting 10 automatic.

faq.q: Why does my child write 236 as 20036?
faq.a: They are writing what they hear — two hundred, thirty, six — and joining the parts. It is very common. Practising expanded form out loud (200 + 30 + 6) and using a three-column place value chart fixes it within a few sessions.

faq.q: What is the hardest part of Grade 2 place value?
faq.a: Numbers with a zero, like 305 or 560. The zero is a placeholder that keeps the other digits in their correct place. Spend extra time on these, as they trip up more children than any other type.
